statischen Gleichungen der Poroelastizität in der Form (vgl. [2])

               − (λ + μ)∇(∇ · u) − μu + α∇P = f                   in B × (0, tend ),            (81)
               ∂
                  (c0 P + α∇ · u) − ∇ · k(∇P − ρf g) = h               in B × (0, tend ).        (82)
               ∂t

Um die Eindeutigkeit der Lösung zu garantieren, müssen diese Gleichungen mit
Anfangs- und Randbedingungen versehen werden. Als mögliche Randbedingungen
können

            u = ud       auf Γd × [0, tend ],        P = Pd     auf Γp × [0, tend ],             (83)
            (σ − αIP )n = tN         auf Γt × [0, tend ],
                                                                                                 (84)
            −k(∇P − g) · n = vf · n             auf Γf × [0, tend ],

gelten. Hierbei erfüllen die verschiedenen Anteile des Randes die Bedingungen
Mathematik als Schlüsseltechnologie zum Verständnis des Systems                             75

                      c0 P (·, 0) + α∇ · u(·, 0) = ζ (·, 0) = ζ0   in B.                  (85)

Es können beispielsweise Anfangsdruck P0 = P (·, 0), Anfangsvolumenkraftdichte

5.2 Numerische Modellierung der Poroelastizität

Obwohl die Existenz einer Lösung durch gewisse Bedingungen garantiert ist, ist es
in den meisten Fällen nicht möglich, eine solche Lösung analytisch zu berechnen.
Stattdessen wird ein numerisches Lösungsverfahren benötigt, um eine adäquate ap-
proximative Lösung zu finden. Wir führen hier ein Lösungsverfahren ein, dass auf
der Methode der Fundamentallösungen beruht, wodurch eine gitter- und integrati-
onsfreie Behandlung ermöglicht wird. Aus Randwertproblemen der Potentialtheorie,
den zeitharmonischen Maxwellgleichungen, der Stokesschen Differentialgleichun-
gen sowie der linearen Elastizitätstheorie ist das Grundkonzept der Methode bekannt.
Ausgangspunkt ist die Rungesche Idee, die ursprünglich in der komplexen Analysis
für die Cauchy–Riemannsche Differentialgleichungen formuliert wurde. Die Idee bei
der Methode der Fundamentallösungen ist, ein System von Fundamentallösungen
für eine gegebene Differentialgleichung auszuwählen, so dass deren Singularitäten
außerhalb des Referenzbereiches positioniert sind. Jede endliche Linearkombination
dieser Fundamentallösungen erfüllt die zugehörigen Differentialgleichungen mit ver-
schwindender rechter Seite und ist somit ein geeigneter Ansatz für die Lösung eines
entsprechenden Anfangs-Randwertproblems. Die Koeffizienten dieses Ansatzes kön-
nen bestimmt werden, indem man verlangt, dass die vorgeschriebenen Anfangs- und
Randwerte approximiert werden müssen, beispielsweise im Sinne eines Abgleichs
der kleinsten Quadrate oder einer Kollokation. Die Grundlagen dieser Idee gehen zu-
rück auf [53, 57, 58]. Die Methode der Fundamentallösungen wird bereits in [41]
formuliert. Ergebnisse im Zusammenhang mit Potentialtheorie, die auch eine Verbin-
dung mit Grenz- und Sprungrelationen bei Schichtpotentialansätzen haben, finden
sich in [26, 27] und den darin enthaltenen Referenzen sowie für schiefachsige Rand-
wertprobleme der mathematischen Geodäsie in [35]. Die wesentlichen Vorteile die-
ser Methode sind, dass sie gitterfrei, integrationsfrei und einfach zu implementieren
ist [54]. Auf der anderen Seite gibt es keinen Hinweis darauf, wie man die genauen
Positionen der Singularitäten wählen muss, um eine möglichst gute Approximation
der gesuchten Lösung zu gewährleisten (vgl. [5, 40, 55]). Die Wahl von geeigne-
ten Punktmengen ist aber entscheidend für die Qualität der Approximation. Oft sind
die auftretenden vollbesetzten linearen Gleichungssysteme schlecht konditioniert und
müssen stabilisiert werden (vgl. z.B. [54]). Allerdings ist das Gesamtaufkommen an
Gleichungen moderat.
    Es ist hilfreich, dass gewisse Systeme von Fundamentallösungen dichte Teilmen-
gen des Lösungsraums einer gegebenen partiellen Differentialgleichung sind. Im Fall
der quasistatischen Poroelastizität kann ein Ansatz, der auf der Methode der Funda-
mentallösungen basiert, in der Form

6 Schlussbemerkungen

Unser Artikel widmet sich der heutigen Geomathematik hinsichtlich ihrer Rolle,
ihrer Aufgaben und ihrem Potential im Hinblick auf Tiefe Geothermie. Die Geo-
mathematik, wie sie bereits in [22] charakterisiert und beschrieben wurde, ver-
steht sich auch im speziellen Anwendungsfalle der „Tiefen Geothermie“ als eine
Brücke zwischen der mathematischen Theorie und der technischen Anwendung.
Eine Besonderheit mathematisch reflektierter geothermischer Forschung liegt dar-
in, dass sie sich vornehmlich mit jenen Gebieten der Erde befasst, die für di-
rekte Messungen nur unzureichend oder auch durch Fernerkungsmethoden nicht
hinreichend zugänglich sind. Inverse Methoden zur mathematischen Auswertung
sind dann unumgänglich. In der tiefen Geothermie laufen sie meist darauf hin-
aus, dass eine geologische Struktur und/oder ein physikalisches Feld nahe der Erd-
oberfläche ausgemessen wird, um sie dann mit mathematischen Methoden in die
interessierenden Tiefenbereiche fortzusetzen („downward and upward continuati-
on“).
   Eine entscheidende Frage ist nun, welche geomathematischen Anforderungen
sich daraus perspektivisch für die nähere Zukunft ableiten. Geomathematik zusam-
men mit dem wissenschaftlichen Konsortium, das sich mit geothermischen Ob-
liegenheiten sowie mit Erdwärmetechnik und Energieausbeutung beschäftigt, kann
und wird helfen, die kritischen Momente geothermischer Projekte zu bewältigen,
d.h. Risikominimierung, wirtschaftliche Effizienz und – so ist zu hoffen auf der
Basis von Wissenschaftlichkeit und verlässlicher Forschungsarbeit – auch sozio-
politische Akzeptanz. Im Zusammenspiel von Risiko und Finanzierbarkeit (sie-
he Abb. 16) sind die Beiträge der Geomathematik innerhalb der beiden ersten
Säulen (nämlich Vorstudien, Potentialverfahren und seismische Exploration) von
enormer Wichtigkeit bei gleichzeitig geringem Kostenaufkommen im Rahmen des
Gesamtprojekts. Dies ist eine entscheidende Beobachtung, aus der sich die Rol-
le der Mathematik als Schlüsseltechnologie für die Tiefe Geothermie kanonisch
ableitet.
Mathematik als Schlüsseltechnologie zum Verständnis des Systems                                          81

lags)


Danksagung H.-Ch. Grunau und M. Grothaus möchten wir für die unterstützenden Bemerkungen und
Hinweise danken. Weiterhin gilt unser Dank C. Heine, Springer Verlag Heidelberg, für die hilfreiche För-
derung geomathematischer Beiträge im Bereich Tiefe Geothermie während der letzten Jahre und seinen
positiven Zuspruch zur Weiterentwicklung unserer Note im „Handbuch Tiefe Geothermie“ zum vorlie-
genden Beitrag. Wir danken dem Projektträger Jülich (PtJ) für die Förderung im Rahmen des „Verbund-
projektes GEOFÜND: Charakterisierung und Weiterentwicklung integrativer Untersuchungsmethoden zur
Quantifizierung des Fündigkeitsrisikos“ (PI: W. Freeeden, FKZ 0325512).

 BOOK REVIEW



Francis Buekenhout and Arjeh M. Cohen:
“Diagram Geometry”
Ergebnisse der Mathematik und ihrer Grenzgebiete, 3. Folge,
vol. 57. Springer-Verlag, 2013, 592 pp


Bernhard Mühlherr


Published online: 12 November 2014
© Deutsche Mathematiker-Vereinigung and Springer-Verlag Berlin Heidelberg 2014




                            Diagram geometry has its roots in the work of Tits dur-
                            ing the 1950s when he was searching for suitable ax-
                            ioms for the combinatorial structures which are nowadays
                            known as buildings. The starting point was the observa-
                            tion that the Dynkin-diagram An has a natural interpre-
                            tation in terms of the n-dimensional projective geometry.
                            The Dynkin-diagram An is associated with the semi-simple
                            group SLn+1 which has a natural action on n-dimensional
                            projective space. Tits’ programme was to look for simi-
                            lar geometries for the semi-simple groups of the remaining
                            types. In view of the interpretation of the diagram An for
                            n-dimensional projective geometry, it was natural to guess
that the diagram should be a central ingredient in the definition of the desired objects.
This led Tits to the definition of a geometry over a Dynkin-diagram. Later on, how-
ever, he realized that the Bruhat decomposition provides a more direct approach to the
link between Lie-theory and combinatorics. This had the effect that diagram geome-
tries only played a minor role in Tits’ theory of buildings and BN-pairs. Although one
can consider buildings as diagram geometries, there is a priori no diagram required in
their definition. Moreover, the slightly more abstract notion of a building turned out
to be much more efficient. As a consequence the theory of diagram geometries was
not pushed further for a while.
    At about the same time there were exciting developments in finite group theory.
Several results of fundamental importance were proved. They suggested that a classi-
fication of the finite simple groups may be within reach. Some years later, several new


            B
B. Mühlherr ( )
Gießen, Germany
e-mail: Bernhard.M.Muehlherr@math.uni-giessen.de
86                                                                             B. Mühlherr

sporadic simple groups were discovered. As a consequence, a lot of group theorists
took part in the big project of classifying the finite simple groups in the 1960s and
1970s. By the end of that period a list of finite simple groups was established which
was conjectured and even announced to be complete. From today’s perspective it is
fair to say that this announcement was made too early. Nevertheless, there is now the
understanding that the proof of the classification theorem for the finite simple groups
is complete and that the list is indeed the list of the original statement. According
to the classification theorem most of the non-abelian finite simple groups are groups
of Lie-type which means that each of them has a BN-pair and hence an action on a
canonical building associated with it. The only exceptions are the alternating groups
and the 26 sporadic groups. The alternating groups are well understood whereas the
sporadic groups are somewhat mysterious. Of course, one would like to ‘explain’ or
‘relate’ them to the infinite families of finite simple groups.
    This question motivated Buekenhout to revisit Tits’ theory of geometries over a
Dynkin diagram. The goal was to modify the original axioms in such a way that one
gets besides the buildings also suitable geometries for the sporadic groups. In his
famous paper Diagrams for geometries and groups he proposed to allow not only
Dynkin diagrams but also other diagrams. He gave several examples of such diagram
geometries for most of the sporadic groups. This programme looked most promis-
ing and provided a large range of exciting questions about groups acting on diagram
geometries. Apart from providing geometries for sporadic groups it also seemed that
these ideas might play an important role in the proof of the classification of finite sim-
ple groups. This was the starting point for a lot of group theorists and geometers to
work systematically on diagram geometries in the 1980s and 1990s. Although several
difficult and beautiful results have been produced through these efforts, the classifi-
cation of finite simple groups has been completed without a satisfactory framework
offered by diagram geometry as the authors write in their introduction. Nevertheless,
incidence geometry has become an independent mathematical subject with its own
questions and techniques. Its interaction with group theory is still a source of inspir-
ing and interesting problems for both areas.
    It is obvious that a review on a book of almost 600 pages cannot provide an ex-
haustive discussion of all the topics covered. This remark applies in particular to the
book under review, because the authors present the material not as an isolated sub-
ject. They provide many examples and remarks which establish connections to other
mathematical areas.
    There are two main goals of the book. The first is to provide the foundations of
diagram geometry and this is roughly speaking the content of the first five chapters.
In the remaining chapters the buildings related to the classical groups are treated from
the incidence-geometric perspective. It becomes clear from the structure of the book
that both subjects are closely related. Nevertheless, it will be convenient to comment
on both parts separately because they are somewhat different in nature.

Foundations of Diagram Geometry Given a geometry over some arbitrary diagram
there is not too much that one can deduce from this information. Therefore, diagram
geometry has to be understood rather as a mathematical language which is convenient
in many different contexts. This language is developed in the first three chapters of
Francis Buekenhout and Arjeh M. Cohen: “Diagram Geometry”                               87

the book. There are no deep theorems, but the basic facts are stated and proved with
great care. This part of the book will serve as a useful reference for anybody using
the language of diagram geometry in his research. The authors provide also a lot
of enlightening examples. Some of them are standard, but even for experts there is
definitively potential for discoveries.
    Whereas the notion of a diagram geometry is far too general for a strong and deep
theory the situation can drastically change with some additional hypotheses. The thin
geometries treated in Chapter 4 of the book constitute one such class of diagram ge-
ometries. In fact, they are automatically geometries over a Coxeter diagram and it
turns out that they are all quotients of a universal geometry which one can associate
to the corresponding Coxeter system. These universal geometries are extremely im-
portant because they are precisely the apartments in Tits’ theory of buildings. More-
over, they are closely related to regular polytopes and tilings which constitute a rich
source of examples for beautiful diagram geometries in the earlier chapters of the
book. Chapter 4 is therefore mainly about Coxeter groups which are treated already
in many textbooks. However, in view of the clear and concise presentation of the ma-
terial it may serve as a most convenient first reference to learn about the basic theory,
especially because it emphasizes geometric aspects of the subject.
    There is another important class of diagram geometries which is treated in Chap-
ter 5 of the book. It was already proved by Tits in the late 1950s that geometries of
type An and projective geometries are essentially the same things. His arguments to
establish this result are probably the most beautiful encountered in diagram geome-
try. In the late 1970s it was Buekenhout who realized that Tits’ ideas are applicable
in much wider context, namely for linear diagram geometries. The authors develop
these ideas in a fairly general framework and make the connection to other areas
of combinatorial geometry, namely the theory of matroids, linear spaces and Steiner
triple systems. Tits’ original result appears as Corollary 5.4.4. in the book.

Geometries Related to Classical Groups and Buildings As already pointed out, the
two parts of the book are quite different in nature. In the first part, the authors present
the foundations of incidence geometry, which was not available in this form in the
existing literature. In contrast to this, the second part is about a most classical subject
which is treated in many existing textbooks. The most prominent among those is the
book La géométrie des groupes classiques of Jean Dieudonné. Therefore, writing a
book on this theme is a challenge because there is the danger that one reproduces or
reorganizes material which is already well presented in the existing literature. This is
definitively not the case for the book under review. In fact, several sections seem more
like parts of a research monograph than parts of a text book. At the same time the
book yields a most beautiful and accessible introduction to the geometry of classical
groups. It provides new and illuminating aspects by developing the theory from a
perspective which has its roots in Tits’ work. Over the last decades this approach was
pushed further by several researchers resulting in an advanced theory of line-spaces.
Many important contributions in this area are due to the authors of the book.
   It is indeed the completely new perspective from which the geometries of classical
groups are approached that makes the book most innovative. In the existing literature
these geometries are constructed from algebraic data. Here one starts with a set of
88                                                                                B. Mühlherr

simple combinatorial axioms and produces the algebra. In the case of projective ge-
ometries this approach is classical. But even in this context the authors have some
interesting new aspects to offer. There is the idea of axiomatizing the projective line
and the authors are able to use this in order to provide an alternate proof of the funda-
mental theorem of projective geometry in Chapter 6. Their contributions to the theory
of polar spaces are even more substantial. Again, it is impossible to highlight them
all. The following three are the most important in the reviewer’s opinion.
1. Point-line approach to polar spaces: Polar spaces have been studied by Veldkamp
   who was able to provide a partial classification, which was then completed by Tits
   in the context of his classification of spherical buildings in 1974. However, the
   combinatorial axioms for polar spaces used by Veldkamp and Tits were somewhat
   technical. It was only later that Buekenhout and Shult were able to show that
   polar spaces can be defined as line spaces satisfying the so-called ‘one or all’-
   axiom. Reading Chapter 7 of the book should convince everybody that this is a
   most astonishing result. Indeed, in this chapter (especially in its Sections 4 and 7)
   the authors introduce the reader to the theory of polar spaces by starting with
   this axiom. The arguments are purely combinatorial, elegant and most efficiently
   organized. By choosing this approach to polar spaces they offer the reader the
   possibility to develop quickly a useful intuition for the geometries of the classical
   groups without even knowing the latter. The book is the first place in the literature
   where this philosophy is pursued thoroughly.
2. Main tools for the classification of polar spaces: There are two central tools in the
   Tits classification of polar spaces of finite rank at least 3. The first is the result that
   each polar space with desarguesian planes is embeddable, the second is a local-
   to-global principle for polar spaces of rank at least 3. The authors use Veldkamp’s
   approach to establish the embeddability result which is completely different from
   Tits’ technique. If the rank is at least 4, this works particularly well and the out-
   come is most elegant. In the rank 3 case one has to work considerably harder, but
   the strategy works also in this case and yields a different proof for Tits’ result
   about embeddability of polar spaces. The authors also prove a modified version
   of the local-global principle which has the advantage that it is also applicable for
   polar spaces of infinite rank. This has the effect that the finite-rank hypothesis in
   the classification of polar spaces can be dropped.
3. Classical geometries and buildings: It is of course well known that projective
   spaces and polar spaces of rank n are ‘buildings of type An , Cn and Dn ’. How-
   ever, there is no place in the literature where this is worked out in detail. This
   is done with great care and in full generality in the book by discussing the sub-
   ject in the context of diagram geometries. Actually, there is much more about this
   connection because the authors treat shadow spaces associated with buildings in
   a wider context. In this way they are able to explain the so called root filtration
   spaces associated with projective spaces and polar spaces. As it is proved in the fi-
   nal section of Chapter 11 one can associate with any irreducible spherical building
   of rank at least 3 a root-filtration space. These structures are important for under-
   standing higher rank Moufang buildings and intimately related to Timmesfeld’s
   theory of abstract root subgroups.
Francis Buekenhout and Arjeh M. Cohen: “Diagram Geometry”                             89

It is already clear from the title that the book does not claim to be a general introduc-
tion to diagram geometry. It focusses on the diagram geometries which are related to
spherical buildings. For this reason several important results (especially from finite
group theory) which are also known under the label ‘diagram geometry’ are not cov-
ered by the book. The focus is clearly on line-spaces related to classical groups and
their buildings. There is a second part in preparation which will focus on the excep-
tional groups. The language of diagram geometry is developed to the extent which is
appropriate for this goal. Within these borders the book provides an exhaustive treat-
ment of the material and makes a lot of connections with other areas, especially in
Chapter 5.
    In each of the 11 chapters of the book, there are exercises and notes organized
in two final sections. Apart from the detailed bibliographical information, the notes
contain much valuable additional information about connections with related topics
and further directions one could pursue.
    The first part of the book and certain later sections constitute an excellent intro-
duction to diagram geometry and polar spaces for graduate students and researchers
who want to get a flavour of the subject. For experts, the book provides a valuable
source of references for basic results on diagram geometry. But there are also ad-
vanced new results, especially in the chapters about polar spaces. The authors give
an alternative, more accessible approach to the classification and cover most impor-
tant additional results. The book provides an approach to the classical groups which
emphasizes their buildings as a main tool to study them. In this way it promotes Tits’
ideas and provides a most valuable complement to the huge literature about classical
groups. The impact of this book for future generations could well be comparable to
the influence of Dieudonné’s book La géométrie des groupes classiques.
